"In medias res" is a Latin phrase. Latin was the language of ancient Rome, and it is the root of many words and expressions still used today in literature, law, science, and academia. The phrase translates directly to "into the middle of things." When you say a story begins in medias res, you are saying it begins right in the middle of the action — not at the very start of the events, and not at the end, but somewhere in the thick of it, where things are already happening.
The Core Idea: What Does It Actually Mean?

Imagine you sit down to watch a movie. Before you even understand who the characters are or what is going on, the screen opens with a car chase at full speed. Bullets are flying, tires are screeching, someone is shouting. You have no idea why this is happening yet. Only later, through flashbacks or conversation, do you find out what led up to this moment.

That is in medias res.

It is a storytelling technique where a story opens in the middle of the action — often at a dramatic, tense, or exciting moment — rather than at the very beginning of the events. The story does not start by introducing the characters calmly, explaining the background, and building slowly toward the conflict. Instead, you are thrown in. The conflict is already alive and breathing when the story begins.

The background information — what happened before the story opened, who the characters are, how the situation came to be — is then revealed gradually as the story progresses, through devices like flashbacks, conversations between characters, or a narrator explaining the past.
Where Did This Term Come From?

The phrase was coined (or at least famously used) by the ancient Roman poet Horace in a work called Ars Poetica, meaning "The Art of Poetry," written around 19–18 BCE. In this work, Horace was giving advice to writers about how to tell stories effectively, and he pointed out that the greatest storytellers do not begin at the very beginning. They plunge the audience straight into the action.

To make his point, Horace referred to Homer, the ancient Greek poet who wrote the Iliad and the Odyssey — two of the oldest and most celebrated epic poems in Western literature. Both poems are brilliant examples of in medias res.

In the Iliad, the Trojan War has already been raging for nine years before the poem even begins. Homer does not start by telling you about the origins of the war — the Judgment of Paris, the abduction of Helen, the assembling of the Greek fleet. He throws you directly into a conflict between the hero Achilles and the Greek commander Agamemnon in the war's tenth year. You learn about earlier events only as the story unfolds.

In the Odyssey, the hero Odysseus has already been wandering the seas for ten years trying to get home after the fall of Troy. The poem does not begin with the fall of Troy. It begins with Odysseus stranded on an island, and you learn about his past adventures later — when he sits down and recounts them himself to a group of people called the Phaeacians.

This was so effective, so artful, that Horace held it up as a model for all storytelling. The term in medias res was born from his observation.
The Opposite of In Medias Res: Ab Ovo

To truly understand in medias res, it helps to know its opposite: ab ovo, which is Latin for "from the egg." A story told ab ovo starts at the absolute beginning — the earliest point in the chain of events. Everything is explained in order, from the very first cause to the final effect, in a neat chronological line.

Horace actually used this very contrast. He said that Homer did not begin "ab ovo" — he did not start from the egg. He began in the middle. And Horace praised this as the superior, more skillful approach.

Think of it this way:

A story about a shipwreck told ab ovo would begin with the ship being built, then the captain being hired, then the journey starting, then the weather turning, and only eventually arriving at the shipwreck itself.

The same story told in medias res would open with people clinging to wreckage in the ocean, waves crashing, survival in doubt — and only later, through a conversation or a flashback, would you learn how the ship was lost.

One approach is slow and methodical. The other is immediate and gripping.
Why Do Writers Use This Technique?

In medias res is not just a fancy trick. It serves several powerful purposes, and understanding why writers use it will help you recognize and appreciate it more deeply.

It creates instant engagement. If a story opens with a battle, a murder, a tense confrontation, or a race against time, you are immediately drawn in. You want to know what happens next. The story has earned your attention from the first line rather than asking you to be patient while it sets things up.

It raises questions that pull you forward. Because you are dropped into the middle without full context, you naturally start asking: Why is this happening? Who are these people? What happened before this moment? These unanswered questions create a kind of suspense that keeps you reading or watching. You are always leaning slightly forward, waiting for the gaps to be filled.

It mirrors how we often experience real life. In real life, when you walk into a room where something important is already happening, you don't get a full explanation of everything that led to that moment. You piece it together from what you see and hear. Stories told in medias res can feel more natural and immediate for this reason.

It respects the reader's intelligence. Rather than over-explaining everything upfront, the writer trusts you to be patient, to hold unanswered questions in your mind, and to assemble the full picture as it is revealed. This creates a more active, satisfying reading experience.

It allows a non-linear structure. Some stories are deliberately not told in chronological order. Starting in the middle gives the writer the freedom to move backward and forward in time, creating a richer, more layered narrative.

Star Wars (1977) opens with a spacecraft already being boarded and attacked. There is no setup explaining who the Empire is, who the Rebellion is, or what the conflict is about. You are in the middle of a battle. Details are filled in as the story progresses.

The Dark Knight (2008) opens with a bank robbery already in progress. You meet the Joker mid-crime. His background, motivations, and history are not explained upfront.

Breaking Bad begins its pilot episode with the main character, Walter White, in a gas mask, driving an RV through the desert in what looks like a desperate situation. You have no idea who he is or how he got there. The story then rewinds and explains.

Hamlet by Shakespeare begins after the death of Hamlet's father is already a recent event. The ghost has already appeared. We do not witness the murder that starts the whole chain of events — it is revealed to us later.

The Odyssey, as discussed, begins with ten years of wandering already behind the hero.

These are wildly different stories from wildly different times, but they share this one technique: they begin in medias res.
How Background Information Gets Filled In

Since the story begins mid-action without full context, writers need to deliver the missing background somehow. There are several standard ways this happens:

A flashback is when the story temporarily goes back in time to show you something that happened before the story began. Films do this frequently with a change in visual tone or an explicit label like "Three Years Earlier."

A character might tell another character about the past through conversation. This is a natural way to deliver information — one character explains to another (and therefore to the reader/viewer) what happened before the story opened.

A narrator — a voice that speaks directly to the reader — can step in and explain the background in their own voice.

Sometimes, information about the past is simply woven into the details of the present scene — the way a character acts, the objects around them, the references they make — and you piece it together yourself.
A Note on Flashbacks vs. In Medias Res

People sometimes confuse these, so it is worth clarifying. In medias res is a structural choice about where a story begins. A flashback is a technique used within a story to show earlier events. The two are related but not the same thing.

A story that begins in medias res will very often use flashbacks to fill in the background — but not always. And a story that begins at the beginning (ab ovo) can still contain flashbacks within it. In medias res is about the opening. Flashbacks are about how a writer moves through time once the story is underway.

Ask yourself this simple question when you start a story, film, or book: Does the story begin before anything has happened yet, or has something already happened?

If you feel like you have been "dropped in" to a situation that is already in progress — if there is tension, conflict, or action present from the very first moment, and you do not yet have the full picture of how things got to this point — then you are almost certainly looking at in medias res.

In medias res means starting a story in the middle of the action. The writer does not begin at the very beginning of the events. Instead, you are placed right into a dramatic moment that is already underway, and the background is revealed to you gradually as the story moves forward. The term comes from Latin and was described by the Roman poet Horace, who praised Homer for using it brilliantly thousands of years ago. Writers use it because it hooks the audience immediately, creates suspense, and makes for a more dynamic and engaging story. It is one of the oldest and most powerful techniques in all of storytelling.
